subChunks.title: Pub/Sub, Point-to-Point, Dead Letters & Idempotency
subChunks.hookHtml: Queues are the glue of distributed systems — they decouple producers from consumers, buffer spikes in load, and enable retry logic for failures. Understanding messaging patterns is essential for any senior engineer building services that communicate asynchronously.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Point-to-Point (Queue)

A message is produced to a queue and consumed by exactly one consumer. Used for task distribution — work items, job queues, command processing. Each message is processed once. Technologies: RabbitMQ (basic queue), AWS SQS, Kafka (with consumer group of one).

Publish-Subscribe (Pub/Sub)

A message is published to a topic and delivered to all subscribers. Used for broadcasting events — 'order placed' notifies inventory, shipping, and billing simultaneously. Each subscriber gets its own copy. Technologies: Kafka topics, Google Pub/Sub, SNS, RabbitMQ fanout exchange.

// Simulating pub/sub with a topic and multiple subscribers
Map<String, List<Consumer<String>>> subscribers = new HashMap<>();

void subscribe(String topic, Consumer<String> handler) {
    subscribers.computeIfAbsent(topic, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(handler);
}

void publish(String topic, String message) {
    subscribers.getOrDefault(topic, List.of())
               .forEach(h -> h.accept(message));
}

// Subscribe
subscribe("order.placed", msg -> System.out.println("Inventory: " + msg));
subscribe("order.placed", msg -> System.out.println("Billing:   " + msg));
// Publish
publish("order.placed", "order-123 qty=5");

Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)

When a message fails processing repeatedly (maxDeliveryAttempts exceeded), it is moved to the Dead Letter Queue rather than being discarded or blocking the main queue. The DLQ allows:

  • Alerting on persistent failures
  • Manual inspection and replay after fixing the bug
  • Preventing a single bad message from blocking all other processing

Message Acknowledgement

At-most-once: message acknowledged before processing. May be lost if consumer crashes. Use for metrics/telemetry where loss is acceptable.

At-least-once: message acknowledged after processing succeeds. May be redelivered if consumer crashes after processing but before ack. Requires idempotent consumers.

Exactly-once: message processed exactly once. Very expensive to guarantee — requires coordination. Kafka transactions and distributed two-phase commit.

Consumer Groups & Scaling

Multiple consumer instances in a consumer group share the partition/queue work. Kafka assigns partitions to consumers in a group — scaling consumers scales throughput horizontally up to the number of partitions.

Backpressure

If consumers are slower than producers, the queue grows unboundedly. Solutions: cap queue depth (reject or block producers), scale consumers, or use bounded queues with drop/block/retry policies.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's spell dispatch system used to process every spell synchronously. When the enchantment server was slow, the whole Academy waited. Then the architects added a queue between requests and processing. Load spikes buffered gracefully. Processing scaled independently. And dead letters caught the malformed spells that would have previously crashed the dispatcher silently.

storyBeats.speaker: Queue Architect Bren
storyBeats.text: Point-to-point vs pub/sub is the first decision. Point-to-point: one message, one processor — task queues, job distribution. Pub/sub: one event, many reactions — order placed triggers inventory, shipping, billing simultaneously. These are fundamentally different communication patterns and each maps to a different technology.

storyBeats.speaker: Queue Architect Bren
storyBeats.text: Dead letter queues are not an afterthought. They are infrastructure. A message that fails three times has something wrong with it — bad data, a bug in the consumer, or an incompatible schema change. Without a DLQ, it either blocks the queue forever or is silently dropped. The DLQ lets you inspect it, fix the consumer, and replay.

storyBeats.speaker: At-least-once delivery — why idempotency matters
Queue Architect Bren
storyBeats.text: Exactly-once delivery is the most expensive guarantee. In most systems you should aim for at-least-once with idempotent consumers instead — it is cheaper and almost always sufficient. Reserve exactly-once for financial systems where even a duplicate processed idempotently might have tax or regulatory implications.

learningObjectives: Distinguish point-to-point (queue) and publish-subscribe (topic) messaging patterns and name a use case for each
Explain the purpose of a Dead Letter Queue and what triggers messages to be sent there
Compare at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once delivery semantics and their trade-offs
Implement a simple in-memory pub/sub dispatcher in Java using a Map of topic to List<Consumer>
commonMistakes: Using pub/sub when only one consumer should process each message — use a queue with consumer group instead
Not handling DLQ alerts — a growing DLQ means silent processing failures accumulating
Assuming at-least-once delivery without making consumers idempotent — duplicate processing causes data corruption
Unbounded queues in production — a slow consumer will eventually cause an OOM if the queue has no depth limit
assessmentCriteria: Can explain when to use pub/sub vs point-to-point with a concrete example for each
Can describe the DLQ pattern and explain what conditions trigger a message to be dead-lettered
Can explain why at-least-once delivery requires idempotent consumers with a concrete failure scenario
Can implement an in-memory pub/sub system demonstrating multi-subscriber fan-out
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain messaging queues to a developer who currently uses direct REST API calls between services. What problems does a queue solve? What new problems does it introduce? When would you choose pub/sub vs point-to-point?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write a MessageQueue class that simulates a pub/sub broker in memory:

  1. Fields: Map<String, List<Consumer<String>>> subscribers and Map<String, List<String>> deadLetterQueue
  2. Method subscribe(String topic, Consumer<String> handler)
  3. Method publish(String topic, String message) that calls each subscriber's handler; if the handler throws any exception, add the message to the DLQ for that topic (use computeIfAbsent)
  4. Method getDlq(String topic) returning the dead letter list for a topic
  5. In main: subscribe two handlers to 'spell.cast'; one prints the message, one throws RuntimeException for any message containing 'bad'. Publish 'Fireball' and 'bad-spell'. Print DLQ contents.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Extend MessageQueue into a class ReliableQueue that supports max retry with DLQ for point-to-point delivery:

  • Field: Map<String, Integer> retryCount tracking attempts per message ID
  • Method enqueue(String msgId, String payload)
  • Method process(String msgId, Consumer<String> handler) that attempts to process the message; if it throws, increments the retry count; if retries >= 3, moves to DLQ and prints 'Dead lettered: msgId'
  • In main: enqueue 'msg-1' with payload 'good', enqueue 'msg-2' with payload 'fail'. Handler throws for 'fail'. Call process 4 times for msg-2. Print final DLQ.

questions.prompt: In messaging systems, what is the purpose of a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)?
options: To store messages that were delivered successfully
To capture messages that failed processing after maximum retries so they can be inspected and replayed
To hold messages that arrived before consumers were ready
To archive all messages for audit purposes
questions.answer: To capture messages that failed processing after maximum retries so they can be inspected and replayed
questions.explanation: A DLQ captures messages that have exceeded their retry limit. This prevents a single bad message from blocking the main queue indefinitely. Operations teams can inspect DLQ contents, identify the root cause, fix the consumer or data, and replay the messages. Without a DLQ, bad messages either cause infinite retries or are silently dropped.

questions.prompt: A payment processing consumer uses at-least-once delivery. The service processes a payment successfully and then crashes before sending the acknowledgement. What happens and what prevents a double charge?
options: The broker re-delivers the message; an idempotency check detects the duplicate and skips reprocessing
The broker automatically rolls back the payment
The consumer restarts and the payment is processed again, causing a double charge
questions.answer: The broker re-delivers the message; an idempotency check detects the duplicate and skips reprocessing
questions.explanation: With at-least-once delivery, re-delivery after a crash is guaranteed. Without idempotency, the payment would be charged twice. The correct pattern: before processing, check if a payment with this message ID was already processed (stored in a DB). If yes, return the previous result. If no, process and store the record. This makes the consumer safe for at-least-once delivery.

questions.prompt: You need to notify three different services (inventory, shipping, billing) every time an order is placed. Which messaging pattern is most appropriate?
options: Point-to-point queue — send three separate messages, one to each service queue
Pub/sub topic — publish one 'order.placed' event; all three services subscribe independently
Request/response REST API — call each service in sequence
Shared database polling — all services poll the orders table for new rows
questions.answer: Pub/sub topic — publish one 'order.placed' event; all three services subscribe independently
questions.explanation: Pub/sub is designed exactly for this: one producer, many consumers each receiving their own copy of the event. Point-to-point with three queues works but requires the producer to know about all downstream consumers — tight coupling. Pub/sub decouples producers from consumers: adding a fourth subscriber requires no changes to the order service.
